title: Chapter 2: The Production Possibilities Frontier & Gains from Trade

questions.topic: Scarcity and the PPF Model
questions.title: Defining the Production Possibilities Frontier and Ceteris Paribus
questions.prompt_template: Which statement accurately defines a society's Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF) and the ceteris paribus conditions held fixed along it?

hints.text: Recall what the PPF measures about output combinations and what must remain constant while drawing a single frontier.
Distinguish productive capacity (resources and technology) from consumer demand or market prices.

options_template.text: The set of all output combinations consumers are willing to purchase at current market prices, holding household income fixed.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Budget-Constraint Confusion): Willingness to purchase at market prices describes a consumer budget line or demand curve, not an economy's aggregate production boundary.

options_template.text: The maximum combinations of two goods or services an economy can produce when all available resources are fully employed using current technology, holding resource supplies and technology fixed.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A single PPF captures maximum feasible output under full employment of finite land, labor, physical capital, and entrepreneurship, holding input quantities and technology constant.

options_template.text: The minimum combinations of inputs required to maintain zero inflation while allowing technology and labor supplies to expand continuously.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Macroeconomic Target Confusion): The PPF maps maximum output of two goods with fixed inputs and technology; it does not allow resources or technology to grow along a single static curve.

options_template.text: The single optimal output mix that maximizes social welfare regardless of how efficiently resources are deployed across industries.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Point Reduction): The PPF represents an entire menu of productively efficient output bundles, not just a single welfare-maximizing point, and requires full resource utilization.

questions.topic: Productive vs. Allocative Efficiency
questions.title: Distinguishing Productive Efficiency from Allocative Efficiency
questions.prompt_template: An economy fully employs every worker and machine along its PPF to produce millions of unwanted cassette tapes rather than needed healthcare and housing. How do economists classify this production point?

hints.text: Check whether resources are wasted or idle, and separately check whether the output mix matches what society values most.
Compare operating on the PPF (productive efficiency) with satisfying MB = MC for society's preferred mix (allocative efficiency).

options_template.text: Both productively efficient and allocatively efficient, because no workers or machines are sitting idle.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Equating Full Employment with Allocative Efficiency): Full utilization guarantees productive efficiency, but allocative efficiency additionally requires producing the specific mix society values most (MB = MC).

options_template.text: Neither productively efficient nor allocatively efficient, because producing unwanted goods automatically places the economy inside the PPF.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Conflating Desirability with Feasibility): A point's location on the PPF depends solely on whether inputs are fully and non-wastefully used, not on whether consumers prefer the chosen bundle.

options_template.text: Productively efficient because it lies on the PPF with zero wasted inputs, yet allocatively inefficient because it fails to match the mix society values most where MB = MC.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Every point on the PPF achieves productive efficiency, but only the single point aligning production with societal preferences (MB = MC) achieves allocative efficiency.

options_template.text: Allocatively efficient because full employment minimizes unit costs, yet productively inefficient because technology is outdated.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reversed Efficiency Definitions): Minimizing resource cost on the PPF is productive efficiency, whereas matching societal value (MB = MC) is allocative efficiency—this option swaps the two concepts.

questions.topic: PPF Zones: Efficient, Inefficient, and Unattainable
questions.title: Economic Meaning of an Interior PPF Point
questions.prompt_template: What does it signify when an economy operates at a point strictly inside its Production Possibilities Frontier?

hints.text: Think about the three zones separated by the PPF boundary: inside, on, and outside.
Consider why actual output falls short of maximum feasible output despite fixed technology and factor supplies.

options_template.text: The bundle is attainable but productively inefficient because productive resources are either unemployed or misallocated across industries.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Any interior point is feasible with current resources and technology, but idle inputs (such as unemployed labor during a recession) or misallocation keep output below the frontier.

options_template.text: The bundle is unattainable under current technology and requires capital accumulation before society can produce it.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Interior-Exterior Inversion): Unattainable bundles lie strictly outside the PPF, whereas bundles strictly inside the PPF are attainable.

options_template.text: The economy has achieved allocative efficiency by conserving scarce resources for future generations rather than using them today.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Conservation Misconception): Leaving labor and machinery idle inside the PPF represents productive waste rather than deliberate intertemporal investment in capital goods.

options_template.text: The economy faces an infinitely high opportunity cost for expanding output of either good.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-vs-Infinite Cost Confusion): Inside the PPF, putting idle resources to work lets society expand both goods without sacrificing either, meaning zero opportunity cost—not infinite cost.

questions.topic: Opportunity Cost Along vs. Inside the PPF
questions.title: Why Trade-Offs Bind on the PPF but Not Inside It
questions.prompt_template: Why does expanding production of Good X always impose an opportunity cost when the economy operates on its PPF, whereas an economy operating strictly inside its PPF can expand both Good X and Good Y simultaneously?

hints.text: Compare the availability of idle resources on the boundary versus in the interior.
On the frontier, where must additional inputs for Good X come from?

options_template.text: Because technological progress automatically occurs whenever an economy starts inside the PPF, eliminating scarcity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Spontaneous Technology Fallacy): Moving from an interior point to the frontier does not involve new technology; it merely puts existing idle inputs to work.

options_template.text: Because opportunity cost only exists in market economies using money prices, not in physical resource models.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Monetary-Only Cost Fallacy): Opportunity cost is a physical real-resource trade-off measured in forgone output of Good Y even without money prices.

options_template.text: Because points on the PPF suffer from misallocated labor, forcing workers to be retrained before switching industries.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Misallocation Inversion): Misallocated or unemployed inputs characterize interior points; points on the PPF already allocate all resources productively.

options_template.text: Because on the PPF all resources are already fully and efficiently employed, so expanding Good X requires withdrawing inputs from Good Y, whereas inside the PPF idle or misallocated inputs can be activated.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Full employment along the frontier creates an unavoidable trade-off, while idle capacity inside the frontier allows simultaneous output gains in both goods with no sacrifice of the other.

questions.topic: Linear vs. Concave PPF Curvature
questions.title: Factor Adaptability and PPF Shape
questions.prompt_template: What underlying assumption about productive resources determines whether a Production Possibilities Frontier is a straight line rather than a curve bowed outward from the origin?

hints.text: Compare how easily land, labor, and machinery transfer between the two industries in each model.
A straight line has a constant slope, meaning constant opportunity cost across all output levels.

options_template.text: A straight-line PPF assumes that resources are unlimited, whereas a bowed-out PPF assumes that scarcity exists.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Scarcity-Shape Confusion): Both linear and concave PPFs slope downward and therefore reflect scarcity and trade-offs.

options_template.text: A straight-line PPF assumes rapid technological growth, whereas a bowed-out PPF holds technology fixed.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Growth-Curvature Confusion): Both linear and concave static PPFs hold technology and factor supplies constant; growth shifts the curve rather than straightening it.

options_template.text: A straight-line PPF assumes resources are equally adaptable between both industries (constant opportunity cost), whereas a bowed-out PPF reflects imperfect factor adaptability (increasing opportunity cost).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Perfect factor substitutability yields a constant slope (linear PPF), whereas specialized resources with imperfect adaptability cause opportunity costs to rise along a concave PPF.

options_template.text: A straight-line PPF occurs only when both goods have identical market prices, whereas a bowed-out PPF occurs when prices differ.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Driven Curvature Fallacy): PPF shape is determined by production technology and factor adaptability, not by output prices.

questions.topic: Law of Increasing Opportunity Cost
questions.title: Mechanism Behind the Law of Increasing Opportunity Cost
questions.prompt_template: Under the Law of Increasing Opportunity Cost, why does the sacrifice of agricultural grain per additional autonomous drone start small and then rise sharply as drone output expands?

hints.text: Think about which workers and resources rational managers reassign first when expanding a new sector.
Consider what happens to productivity in grain versus drones as progressively less suitable inputs are pulled into drone assembly.

options_template.text: Managers first reassign resources best suited to drone manufacturing (such as robotics engineers) while leaving fertile farmland in agriculture; further expansion forces the use of inputs increasingly better suited to farming than aerospace.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Rational sequencing deploys the lowest-opportunity-cost inputs first; pushing further requires converting specialized farm resources that sacrifice large quantities of grain for small drone gains.

options_template.text: Workers automatically become less motivated as total output rises, reducing productivity equally across every sector of the economy.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Uniform Fatigue Fallacy): Increasing opportunity cost stems from heterogeneous, specialized factors across industries, not uniform worker fatigue.

options_template.text: Managers randomly pull inputs out of farming without regard to skill, causing unpredictable spikes in opportunity cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Random Allocation Assumption): The PPF assumes productive efficiency—managers systematically allocate inputs to their highest comparative productivity, not randomly.

options_template.text: Producing more drones destroys existing physical capital in the agricultural sector, shrinking the economy's total land supply.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Resource-Destruction Fallacy): Movement along a static PPF reallocates fixed resources between industries; it does not destroy total factor endowments.

questions.topic: Marginal Rate of Transformation (MRT)
questions.title: Defining the Marginal Rate of Transformation
questions.prompt_template: Along a smooth, twice-differentiable Production Possibilities Frontier Y = f(X), what does the Marginal Rate of Transformation (MRT_XY) measure?

hints.text: Recall how the instantaneous slope of the PPF relates to marginal production costs of Good X and Good Y.
Check the sign convention: MRT_XY is defined as the positive magnitude -dY/dX.

options_template.text: The ratio of total output of Good Y to total output of Good X at any interior point inside the frontier.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Average-vs-Marginal Confusion): MRT is a marginal trade-off measured by the instantaneous slope along the frontier, not a ratio of total output levels inside the PPF.

options_template.text: The instantaneous rate at which Good Y must be sacrificed to produce one additional unit of Good X, equal to -dY/dX and to the ratio of marginal production costs MC_X / MC_Y.
options_template.feedback: Correct. MRT_XY = -dY/dX = MC_X / MC_Y captures the exact instantaneous marginal opportunity cost of Good X in terms of Good Y along a smooth PPF.

options_template.text: The percentage increase in total factor productivity generated when the PPF shifts outward over time.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Growth-Rate Confusion): MRT measures the trade-off slope along a single static PPF, not the dynamic shift rate of economic growth.

options_template.text: The ratio of marginal cost of Good Y to marginal cost of Good X, equal to MC_Y / MC_X.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Marginal Cost Ratio): Because producing an extra dollar's worth of resources in X pulls MC_X / MC_Y units out of Y, MRT_XY equals MC_X / MC_Y, not its reciprocal.

questions.topic: Drivers of Long-Run Economic Growth
questions.title: Four Primary Forces Shifting the PPF Outward
questions.prompt_template: Which combination lists the four primary drivers that expand an economy's long-run productive capacity and shift its PPF outward?

hints.text: Focus on supply-side expansions in factor quantities, factor quality, and production technology.
Exclude short-run demand or utilization changes that merely move the economy toward an existing frontier.

options_template.text: Lower unemployment rates, higher consumer spending, tighter tariff barriers, and fixed factory utilization.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-and-Utilization Confusion): Reducing unemployment moves the economy from inside the PPF toward the existing frontier, and tariffs do not expand domestic production capacity.

options_template.text: Higher retail prices, reduced saving rates, stricter autarky rules, and shorter working hours.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Nominal-and-Contractionary Confusion): Higher prices are nominal changes, while lower saving and fewer labor hours restrict rather than expand productive capacity.

options_template.text: Converting capital-goods factories into consumer-goods factories, eliminating comparative advantage, and increasing government transfer payments.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reallocation-as-Growth Fallacy): Shifting from capital goods to consumer goods moves along today's PPF and actually slows future outward PPF growth.

options_template.text: Physical capital accumulation, labor force growth, human capital investment, and technological innovation.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Expanding physical capital, growing the workforce, upgrading worker skills and health (human capital), and improving total factor productivity via technology all shift the PPF outward.

questions.topic: Economic Recovery vs. Economic Growth
questions.title: Distinguishing Short-Run Recovery from Long-Run Growth
questions.prompt_template: How does short-run economic recovery from a recession differ conceptually from long-run economic growth in the PPF framework?

hints.text: Ask whether the economy's maximum productive capacity changes during a recession recovery.
Contrast improving utilization of existing resources against expanding total potential output.

options_template.text: Short-run recovery shifts the PPF outward permanently, whereas long-run growth moves the economy clockwise along a fixed PPF.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reversed Dynamics): Shifting the PPF outward represents long-run growth, whereas clockwise movement along the PPF is a change in output mix, not growth.

options_template.text: Short-run recovery moves the economy from an interior point toward the existing PPF by re-employing idle inputs, whereas long-run growth shifts the entire PPF outward by expanding productive capacity.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Recovery improves utilization of existing labor and capital without expanding capacity; long-run growth expands maximum feasible output beyond the previous frontier.

options_template.text: Short-run recovery requires technological breakthroughs in every sector, whereas long-run growth only requires reducing cyclical unemployment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Swapped Mechanisms): Reducing cyclical unemployment drives short-run recovery inside the PPF, whereas technological progress drives long-run outward shifts.

options_template.text: There is no conceptual difference; any increase in total GDP automatically shifts the PPF outward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (GDP-Equals-Capacity Fallacy): Rising GDP during a recovery reflects higher utilization of idle resources, not an expansion of the economy's maximum frontier.

questions.topic: Autarky and Gains from Trade
questions.title: Consumption Constraint Under Autarky
questions.prompt_template: In economic analysis, what is 'autarky,' and what constraint does it impose on a region's Consumption Possibilities Frontier (CPF)?

hints.text: Recall the Greek root of autarky (self-sufficiency) and its implication for imports and exports.
Without trade, can a region ever consume a bundle that it does not physically produce itself?

options_template.text: A trade bloc with zero tariffs, which causes the region's CPF to pivot strictly outside its domestic PPF.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Free-Trade Inversion): Free trade expands the CPF outside the PPF; autarky is the exact opposite—complete isolation with zero trade.

options_template.text: A policy of specializing exclusively in one good while importing all other goods from lower-cost trading partners.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Specialization Confusion): Complete specialization relies on external trade, whereas autarky forces a region to produce everything it consumes domestically.

options_template.text: Complete economic self-sufficiency without external trade, which traps a region's CPF so that it coincides exactly with its domestic PPF.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Under autarky, a region can only consume what it produces domestically, so its Consumption Possibilities Frontier cannot extend beyond its own Production Possibilities Frontier.

options_template.text: An economy operating inside its PPF during a recession, where imports permanently exceed exports.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Recession-Autarky Confusion): Autarky describes the absence of trade rather than idle domestic capacity; an autarkic economy can still be productively efficient on its PPF.

questions.topic: Absolute vs. Comparative Advantage
questions.title: Defining Absolute Advantage vs. Comparative Advantage
questions.prompt_template: What is the fundamental distinction between absolute advantage and comparative advantage in David Ricardo's trade model?

hints.text: Focus on total output per unit of input versus relative opportunity cost.
Remember which of the two concepts governs mutually beneficial specialization and trade.

options_template.text: Absolute advantage measures the ability to produce more output with identical inputs, whereas comparative advantage measures the ability to produce a good at a lower domestic opportunity cost.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Absolute advantage compares raw productivity levels across producers, whereas comparative advantage compares relative sacrifices (domestic opportunity costs) and determines specialization.

options_template.text: Absolute advantage applies only to agricultural goods, whereas comparative advantage applies only to high-technology manufactured goods.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sectoral-Boundary Fallacy): Both concepts apply universally across all goods and services—agriculture, manufacturing, software, and services alike.

options_template.text: Absolute advantage measures lower domestic opportunity cost, whereas comparative advantage measures higher total output from the same labor force.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Swapped Definitions): This option reverses the canonical definitions—total output per input is absolute advantage, and lower opportunity cost is comparative advantage.

options_template.text: Absolute advantage determines mutually beneficial Terms of Trade, whereas comparative advantage only determines which country holds larger gold reserves.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Mercantilist Fallacy): Ricardian comparative advantage—not absolute productivity or bullion reserves—governs valid Terms of Trade and mutual gains from trade.

questions.topic: Reciprocal Nature of Comparative Advantage
questions.title: Why One Region Cannot Hold Comparative Advantage in Both Goods
questions.prompt_template: In a two-region, two-good Ricardian model where domestic opportunity costs differ between regions, why is it mathematically impossible for one region to hold a comparative advantage in both goods?

hints.text: Write down the algebraic relationship between a region's opportunity cost of Good X and its opportunity cost of Good Y.
If one positive fraction is smaller than another, what must be true of their reciprocals?

options_template.text: Because international trade agreements legally prohibit any nation from exporting more than one commodity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Legal-Constraint Misconception): The impossibility is a purely mathematical property of opportunity cost ratios, not a result of legal treaties.

options_template.text: Because neither region is permitted to have an absolute advantage in both goods simultaneously.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Absolute-Advantage Conflation): One region CAN easily hold an absolute advantage in both goods, yet it still cannot hold a comparative advantage in both.

options_template.text: Because total global production is fixed, so gains by one region must come at the direct expense of the other.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Sum Fallacy): Ricardian trade is positive-sum, expanding total global output; the impossibility stems from reciprocal opportunity cost ratios.

options_template.text: Because the opportunity cost of Good Y is the exact reciprocal of the opportunity cost of Good X; having a lower opportunity cost in X mathematically guarantees a higher opportunity cost in Y.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Since OC_1Y = 1 / OC_1X, if Region A has OC_1X < Region B's OC_1X, then automatically Region A's OC_1Y > Region B's OC_1Y, giving Region B comparative advantage in Y.

questions.topic: Ricardian Model Assumptions & Terms of Trade
questions.title: Core Assumptions of the Baseline Ricardian Model and TOT Rule
questions.prompt_template: Which set of simplifying assumptions underlies the baseline Ricardian gains-from-trade model, and what condition must the Terms of Trade (TOT) satisfy for both regions to benefit?

hints.text: Recall the three baseline Ricardian assumptions regarding PPF shape, resource employment, and trade frictions.
Check where TOT must sit relative to the exporter's and importer's domestic opportunity costs.

options_template.text: Increasing opportunity costs, chronic unemployment, and uniform import tariffs; TOT must exceed both regions' domestic opportunity costs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Assumption-and-Bound Error): The baseline Ricardian model assumes constant opportunity costs, full employment, and zero tariffs, and a TOT above both domestic costs would harm the importer.

options_template.text: Constant domestic opportunity costs along linear PPFs, full employment in both regions, and zero transportation or tariff costs; TOT must lie strictly between the exporter's and importer's domestic opportunity costs.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The canonical Ricardian model assumes linear PPFs, full employment, and frictionless trade, and guarantees mutual gains whenever OC_Exporter < TOT < OC_Importer.

options_template.text: Constant domestic opportunity costs, zero saving, and identical technology across regions; TOT must exactly equal the exporter's domestic opportunity cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Gain Boundary Error): Identical opportunity costs eliminate comparative advantage, and setting TOT equal to the exporter's OC leaves the exporter with zero gain from trade.

options_template.text: Bowed-out PPFs, fixed money wages, and prohibitive shipping costs; TOT must lie strictly below both regions' domestic opportunity costs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Exporter-Loss Bound Error): A TOT below both regions' domestic opportunity costs would force the exporter to sell below its own production cost, preventing voluntary trade.

questions.topic: Interpreting Movements on Figure 2.1
questions.title: Moving from Interior Point U(20, 40) to Frontier Point A(30, 40)
questions.prompt_template: Along the linear PPF Y = 100 - 2X between Electric Vehicles (X, thousands) and Battery Packs (Y, thousands), an economy moves from interior point U(20, 40) horizontally to efficient point A(30, 40). What does this graphical movement represent?

hints.text: Compare the coordinates of U(20, 40) and A(30, 40): does Battery Pack output fall as Electric Vehicle output rises?
Check whether point U lies inside or on the line Y = 100 - 2X.

options_template.text: Putting idle or misallocated resources to work to expand Electric Vehicle output by 10 thousand units while sacrificing zero Battery Packs.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because U(20, 40) lies strictly inside the PPF (where Y_max(20) = 60), moving horizontally to A(30, 40) eliminates productive inefficiency with zero opportunity cost in Battery Packs.

options_template.text: An outward shift of the PPF caused by a technological breakthrough in Electric Vehicle assembly.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift-vs-Utilization Confusion): The PPF equation Y = 100 - 2X has not changed; moving from inside the frontier to A(30, 40) is improved utilization, not an outward shift.

options_template.text: A movement along the PPF that imposes an opportunity cost of 20 thousand Battery Packs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Interior-as-Frontier Fallacy): Because Battery Pack production remains constant at 40 thousand, no Battery Packs are sacrificed; U was not on the frontier.

options_template.text: A move into the unattainable region that requires importing Battery Packs from abroad.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Frontier-as-Unattainable Confusion): At X = 30, Y_max = 100 - 2(30) = 40, so A(30, 40) lies directly on the domestic frontier and is fully attainable without trade.

questions.topic: Linear PPF Intercepts and Slope
questions.title: Graphical Meaning of Intercepts and Slope Magnitude on a Linear PPF
questions.prompt_template: On a graph showing a downward-sloping straight-line PPF with Electric Vehicles (X) on the horizontal axis and Battery Packs (Y) on the vertical axis, what do the vertical intercept, horizontal intercept, and absolute value of the slope represent?

hints.text: At the vertical intercept, X = 0; at the horizontal intercept, Y = 0.
Remember that rise over run is Delta Y / Delta X, so its magnitude measures how many units of Y are given up per unit of X.

options_template.text: The vertical intercept shows minimum Battery output, the horizontal intercept shows minimum EV output, and the slope magnitude shows total labor hours.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Minimum-vs-Maximum Inversion): The intercepts measure maximum feasible production when 100% of resources are devoted to a single good, not minimum output.

options_template.text: The intercepts show market equilibrium prices of the two goods, and the slope magnitude shows the constant opportunity cost of producing 1 Battery Pack.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-and-Axis Inversion): PPF axes measure physical output quantities, not prices, and |Delta Y / Delta X| is the opportunity cost of the horizontal-axis good (EVs), not the vertical-axis good.

options_template.text: The vertical intercept shows maximum Battery output when X = 0, the horizontal intercept shows maximum EV output when Y = 0, and the slope magnitude |Delta Y / Delta X| shows the constant opportunity cost of 1 EV in terms of Battery Packs.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Intercepts represent complete specialization in either good, and the constant absolute slope |Delta Y / Delta X| equals the constant opportunity cost of each additional horizontal-axis unit.

options_template.text: The vertical intercept shows allocative efficiency, the horizontal intercept shows productive efficiency, and the slope magnitude measures the rate of long-run economic growth.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Concept-Mapping Confusion): Every point along the line is productively efficient, and slope magnitude captures the static trade-off rate rather than dynamic growth.

questions.topic: Visualizing Increasing Opportunity Cost
questions.title: Steepening Step-Down Triangles Along a Concave PPF
questions.prompt_template: Along the bowed-out PPF Y = 100 - X^2 (Drones X on the horizontal axis, Grain Y on the vertical axis), equal rightward steps of Delta X = +2 thousand drones are plotted from B(2, 96) to C(4, 84) and from D(6, 64) to E(8, 36). What visual pattern appears in the step-down triangles, and what does it illustrate?

hints.text: Compare the vertical drop from B to C (-12) with the vertical drop from D to E (-28) for the exact same horizontal step (+2).
Connect the growing vertical drop per fixed horizontal step to the curvature of the frontier.

options_template.text: The vertical drops shrink as X increases, illustrating decreasing opportunity cost from economies of scale.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Convex-vs-Concave Confusion): Shrinking vertical drops would produce a curve bowed inward (convex), whereas a concave PPF exhibits progressively larger vertical drops.

options_template.text: The vertical drops remain identical for every Delta X = +2 step, illustrating constant factor adaptability.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Linear-PPF Projection): Equal vertical drops occur only along a straight-line PPF; along Y = 100 - X^2, the vertical drop grows from 12 to 28.

options_template.text: The horizontal steps grow wider while the vertical drops stay constant, illustrating balanced economic growth.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Axis-and-Shift Misreading): The horizontal steps are held fixed at +2 along a single static curve; the vertical sacrifice grows steeper.

options_template.text: The vertical drops become progressively taller (from -12 to -28) for the same +2 horizontal gain, visually illustrating the Law of Increasing Opportunity Cost.
options_template.feedback: Correct. As the economy moves rightward along a concave PPF, the curve grows steeper, so equal increases in Drones require increasingly large sacrifices of Grain.

questions.topic: Calculus Geometry of PPF Concavity
questions.title: Graphical Meaning of the Second Derivative d^2Y/dX^2 < 0
questions.prompt_template: For a smooth Production Possibilities Frontier Y = f(X), what graphical property is proved when the second derivative satisfies d^2Y/dX^2 < 0 across the entire domain?

hints.text: Recall how the derivative of the slope (-dY/dX = MRT) behaves when d^2Y/dX^2 is negative.
If dY/dX becomes more negative as X rises, which way does the curve bend relative to the origin?

options_template.text: The PPF is a downward-sloping straight line whose opportunity cost is constant at every output level.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Curvature Confusion): A straight-line PPF has zero second derivative (d^2Y/dX^2 = 0), not a strictly negative second derivative.

options_template.text: The PPF is strictly concave (bowed outward from the origin), meaning its slope grows steeper in magnitude and MRT_XY strictly increases as X expands.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because d(MRT_XY)/dX = d(-dY/dX)/dX = -d^2Y/dX^2 > 0, a negative second derivative proves strict outward concavity and rising marginal opportunity cost.

options_template.text: The PPF is bowed inward toward the origin (convex), meaning opportunity cost falls as more X is produced.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign-of-Concavity Inversion): A curve bowed inward toward the origin has a positive second derivative (d^2Y/dX^2 > 0), not a negative one.

options_template.text: The PPF is upward-sloping, meaning the economy can produce more of Good Y whenever it produces more of Good X.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (First-vs-Second Derivative Confusion): The sign of the slope is determined by the first derivative (dY/dX < 0), whereas d^2Y/dX^2 governs curvature.

questions.topic: Movements Along vs. Shifts of the PPF
questions.title: Reallocation Along the Frontier vs. Capacity Expansion
questions.prompt_template: Suppose an economy operating at full employment reallocates engineers and factory floor space from producing consumer automobiles to producing utility-scale wind turbines, with no change in total resources or technology. How is this represented on a PPF diagram?

hints.text: Check whether total resource supplies or production technology changed.
If the economy starts at full employment on the PPF and reallocates inputs, does the curve move or does the operating point move?

options_template.text: As a movement along the existing PPF from one productively efficient point to another, with no shift of the frontier itself.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Reallocating existing fully employed inputs between sectors changes the output mix along the current frontier without expanding total productive capacity.

options_template.text: As a parallel outward shift of the entire PPF because wind turbines represent clean energy.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reallocation-as-Growth Fallacy): Merely shifting existing resources into a new industry does not shift today's PPF outward; it moves along the existing boundary.

options_template.text: As a movement from a point on the PPF to an interior point inside the PPF due to higher opportunity costs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Trade-Off-as-Inefficiency Fallacy): Paying an opportunity cost along the frontier is completely consistent with full employment and productive efficiency.

options_template.text: As an outward rotation of only the wind-turbine intercept while keeping the automobile intercept fixed.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Biased-Innovation Confusion): A pivot of one intercept requires a sector-specific technological breakthrough or specialized resource increase, not simple reallocation of existing inputs.

questions.topic: Broad Economic Growth Shifts
questions.title: Graphical Effect of Economy-Wide General-Purpose Innovation
questions.prompt_template: In a PPF diagram showing Good X on the horizontal axis and Good Y on the vertical axis, how does an economy-wide expansion in human capital (such as universal vocational training) or general-purpose technology affect the frontier?

hints.text: Ask whether a general-purpose improvement raises productivity in just one industry or in both industries.
Compare Panel (a) and Panel (b) of Figure 2.3 in the chapter.

options_template.text: It rotates only the horizontal intercept outward while leaving the vertical intercept anchored.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Biased-Shift Confusion): Anchoring one intercept describes a sector-specific innovation affecting only Good X, not an economy-wide productivity gain.

options_template.text: It leaves the PPF stationary and moves the economy along the curve toward the Good X intercept.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement-vs-Shift Confusion): Expanding human capital or general-purpose technology alters the ceteris paribus determinants of capacity, shifting the curve itself.

options_template.text: It shifts the entire PPF outward so that both the horizontal and vertical intercepts increase, making previously unattainable bundles feasible.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Broad increases in resources, human capital, or general-purpose technology raise maximum feasible output in both sectors, shifting the entire frontier outward from PPF_0 to PPF_1.

options_template.text: It flattens a concave PPF into a straight line without changing either intercept.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shape-Only Misconception): General-purpose growth expands total capacity (raising both intercepts) rather than merely altering curvature at fixed intercepts.

questions.topic: Sector-Biased Technological Progress
questions.title: Graphical Pivot from Sector-Specific Innovation in Good X
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a breakthrough in automated lithography raises labor productivity exclusively in microchip fabrication (Good X, horizontal axis) while leaving agricultural grain productivity (Good Y, vertical axis) completely unchanged. How does the PPF shift graphically?

hints.text: Check what happens to maximum Grain output if 100% of resources are devoted to Grain (X = 0).
Check what happens to maximum Microchip output if 100% of resources are devoted to Microchips (Y = 0).

options_template.text: Both intercepts shift outward by the exact same percentage, keeping the slope identical everywhere.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Symmetric-Shift Assumption): Because grain technology did not improve, allocating all inputs to grain yields the exact same maximum grain output as before.

options_template.text: The vertical intercept shifts outward while the horizontal intercept remains fixed.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Axis-Reversal Error): Microchips (Good X) are on the horizontal axis, so the horizontal intercept expands while the vertical grain intercept stays anchored.

options_template.text: The PPF shifts inward along the vertical axis because workers immediately abandon agriculture.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Capacity-Contraction Fallacy): Technological progress in one sector never reduces maximum potential output in another sector if all resources were devoted to it.

options_template.text: The PPF pivots outward along the horizontal axis—raising the Good X intercept while anchoring the Good Y intercept at its original value.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Sector-biased innovation in Good X expands maximum X output without altering maximum Y output at X = 0, rotating the frontier outward from the vertical intercept.

questions.topic: Inward PPF Shifts vs. Recessions
questions.title: Distinguishing Capital Destruction from Cyclical Unemployment on a PPF
questions.prompt_template: Compare two adverse shocks: Shock 1 is a severe economic recession that leaves factories intact but causes widespread worker layoffs; Shock 2 is a catastrophic earthquake that physically destroys highways, power grids, and industrial factories. How are these two shocks depicted graphically?

hints.text: Ask in each case whether maximum physical productive capacity decreased, or whether existing capacity merely became underutilized.
Contrast a shift of the curve inward versus a movement of the operating point inside an unchanged curve.

options_template.text: Both shocks shift the entire PPF inward because actual output falls in both cases.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Output-Equals-Frontier Fallacy): A drop in actual output from layoffs does not destroy productive capacity; only a loss of resources or technology shifts the PPF inward.

options_template.text: Shock 1 moves the operating point from the PPF to an interior point inside an unchanged frontier, whereas Shock 2 shifts the entire PPF inward.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Cyclical unemployment underutilizes intact resources (interior point), whereas physical destruction of capital and infrastructure reduces maximum feasible output (inward PPF shift).

options_template.text: Shock 1 shifts the entire PPF inward, whereas Shock 2 moves the economy clockwise along a fixed PPF.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Swapped Shock Effects): Physical destruction shrinks capacity (inward shift), while cyclical unemployment creates an interior inefficiency rather than a capacity loss.

options_template.text: Neither shock affects the PPF or the operating point because technology remains unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Technology-Only Capacity Fallacy): Both actual resource utilization (recession) and physical capital stock (earthquake) directly affect the PPF diagram.

questions.topic: Capital vs. Consumption Goods Growth Trade-Off
questions.title: Intertemporal PPF Shifts from Capital Accumulation
questions.prompt_template: Two identical economies start on the exact same PPF_0 with Capital Goods on the vertical axis and Consumption Goods on the horizontal axis. Economy A chooses a point high on the vertical axis (heavy capital investment), while Economy B chooses a point near the horizontal axis (heavy current consumption). What graphical outcome is predicted ten years later?

hints.text: Recall how physical capital accumulation affects future productive capacity.
Which economy will have a larger stock of factories, power grids, and machinery a decade from now?

options_template.text: Economy A's PPF will have shifted strictly farther outward than Economy B's PPF, giving Economy A larger future capacity for both capital and consumption goods.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Devoting a larger share of today's output to capital goods accelerates physical capital accumulation, driving a larger outward shift of future productive capacity.

options_template.text: Economy B's PPF will shift farther outward because higher current consumption directly creates more factories.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Consumption-as-Investment Confusion): Current consumption satisfies immediate wants but does not add to the stock of productive machinery and infrastructure.

options_template.text: Both economies will share the exact same PPF ten years later because both started on the same PPF_0 and achieved productive efficiency.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Static-Efficiency Fallacy): Two productively efficient points today carry different dynamic consequences depending on how much output is invested in new capital.

options_template.text: Economy A's PPF will pivot inward along the consumption axis because investing in capital permanently reduces future consumption capacity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Short-Run vs. Long-Run Trade-Off Confusion): Investing in capital lowers current consumption, but the expanded capital stock increases future capacity for both goods.

questions.topic: Consumption Possibilities Frontier (NorCal Panel)
questions.title: Pivoting NorCal's CPF Outward via Specialization and Trade
questions.prompt_template: In Figure 2.4 Panel (a), NorCal has a linear PPF from (0, 80) to (40, 0) between Microchips (X, millions) and Avocados (Y, millions). NorCal specializes completely in Microchips at (40, 0) and trades at TOT = 3 Avocados per 1 Microchip. How does NorCal's Consumption Possibilities Frontier (CPF) appear relative to its PPF?

hints.text: Identify the specialization point that remains anchored on both the PPF and the CPF.
Calculate how many Avocados NorCal could obtain if it exported all 40 million Microchips at 3 Avocados per Microchip.

options_template.text: It shifts parallel inward below the PPF because exporting Microchips reduces domestic consumption.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Export-Loss Fallacy): Voluntary trade at TOT = 3Y/1X pays NorCal more Avocados per Microchip than its domestic opportunity cost of 2Y/1X, expanding consumption possibilities.

options_template.text: It remains anchored at the vertical intercept (0, 80) and pivots outward to a horizontal intercept of (120, 0).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Pivot Axis): NorCal specializes in Microchips at (40, 0), so the horizontal intercept (40, 0) stays anchored while the vertical Avocado intercept pivots upward.

options_template.text: It stays anchored at NorCal's specialization point (40, 0) and pivots upward to a vertical intercept of (0, 120), lying strictly outside the PPF for all positive Avocado consumption.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Producing 40M Microchips and trading at TOT = 3Y/1X yields a maximum of 40 x 3 = 120M Avocados, pivoting CPF_NorCal strictly above PPF_NorCal from (40, 0) to (0, 120).

options_template.text: It coincides identically with NorCal's domestic PPF because trade cannot expand domestic production capacity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (PPF-CPF Conflation): Although trade does not shift the domestic PPF, specialization plus mutually beneficial TOT expands the CPF strictly beyond the domestic PPF.

questions.topic: Consumption Possibilities Frontier (SoCal Panel)
questions.title: Graphical Interpretation of SoCal's CPF and Its Slope
questions.prompt_template: In Figure 2.4 Panel (b), SoCal's PPF runs from (0, 120) to (30, 0) (Microchips X, Avocados Y). SoCal specializes in Avocados at (0, 120) and trades at TOT = 3 Avocados per 1 Microchip, generating a CPF from (0, 120) to (40, 0). What is the graphical significance of the slope magnitude of CPF_SoCal compared to PPF_SoCal?

hints.text: Compute the slope magnitude of PPF_SoCal (120 / 30 = 4) and compare it to the slope magnitude of CPF_SoCal (120 / 40 = 3).
Remember that a flatter line anchored at (0, 120) swings outward to the right.

options_template.text: CPF_SoCal is steeper than PPF_SoCal (slope magnitude 4 vs. 3), meaning SoCal must give up more Avocados per Microchip with trade.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Steepness-Inversion Error): PPF_SoCal has slope magnitude 4, whereas CPF_SoCal has a flatter slope magnitude of 3 (the TOT), making Microchips cheaper for SoCal.

options_template.text: CPF_SoCal has a slope magnitude of 0.33, representing SoCal's new domestic opportunity cost after technological growth.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reciprocal-and-Growth Confusion): The vertical-over-horizontal slope magnitude is 120 / 40 = 3 (the TOT), not 1/3, and trade does not alter domestic production technology.

options_template.text: CPF_SoCal is parallel to PPF_SoCal because both regions use the same resource units.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Parallel-CPF Misconception): A CPF can lie outside a linear PPF only if its slope (TOT = 3) differs from the domestic PPF slope (4), causing the line to pivot rather than shift parallel.

options_template.text: CPF_SoCal is flatter than PPF_SoCal (slope magnitude equals TOT = 3 < domestic OC of 4), pivoting outward from (0, 120) because SoCal acquires each Microchip for 3 Avocados instead of sacrificing 4 domestically.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because TOT = 3 < 4, SoCal's CPF pivots rightward from (0, 120) to (40, 0), giving SoCal access to Microchip-Avocado bundles unattainable in autarky.

questions.topic: Visual Comparison of Linear PPF Slopes
questions.title: Inferring Comparative Advantage Directly from PPF Slopes
questions.prompt_template: Two regions, Region P and Region Q, have linear PPFs plotted on identical axes with Good X on the horizontal axis and Good Y on the vertical axis. Region P's PPF is noticeably flatter than Region Q's PPF. What can be concluded immediately about comparative advantage?

hints.text: Translate 'flatter' and 'steeper' into the magnitude of the slope |Delta Y / Delta X|.
Remember that |Delta Y / Delta X| equals the domestic opportunity cost of the horizontal-axis good X.

options_template.text: Region Q has the comparative advantage in Good X because its steeper PPF indicates higher total productivity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Steepness-as-Productivity Fallacy): A steeper PPF means a higher opportunity cost of Good X (more Y sacrificed per X), giving Region Q a comparative disadvantage in X.

options_template.text: Region P has the comparative advantage in Good X (smaller |Delta Y / Delta X|), while Region Q has the comparative advantage in Good Y.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A flatter PPF means Region P sacrifices fewer units of Y per unit of X (lower OC_1X), establishing P's comparative advantage in X and Q's comparative advantage in Y.

options_template.text: Region P has the absolute advantage in both goods because a flatter slope requires fewer inputs per unit of output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Determines-Absolute-Advantage Fallacy): Slope alone reflects only relative opportunity costs, not intercept heights, so you cannot deduce absolute advantage from slope alone.

options_template.text: Neither region can gain from trade unless their PPFs intersect at a common autarky bundle.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intersection-Requirement Myth): Gains from trade require only different PPF slopes (different opportunity costs), regardless of whether the two PPFs cross.

questions.topic: Terms of Trade Shifts and CPF Rotation
questions.title: How an Improvement in Terms of Trade Rotates an Exporter's CPF
questions.prompt_template: Suppose NorCal (domestic OC = 2Y per 1X) specializes in Good X at (40, 0) and trades with SoCal (domestic OC = 4Y per 1X). Initially, they trade at TOT = 3Y per 1X. If negotiations shift the Terms of Trade to TOT = 3.5Y per 1X, how do both regions' Consumption Possibilities Frontiers rotate graphically?

hints.text: Check which region receives more Avocados (Y) per Microchip (X) exported when TOT rises from 3 to 3.5.
Check how each CPF pivots around its respective specialization intercept: (40, 0) for NorCal and (0, 120) for SoCal.

options_template.text: NorCal's CPF pivots further outward (vertical intercept rises from 120 to 140), while SoCal's CPF pivots slightly inward toward its PPF (horizontal intercept falls from 40 to about 34.3), though both CPFs still remain strictly outside their domestic PPFs.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A higher TOT (closer to SoCal's OC of 4) increases NorCal's maximum Y from 40 x 3 = 120 to 40 x 3.5 = 140 and reduces SoCal's maximum X from 120 / 3 = 40 to 120 / 3.5 ≈ 34.3, while still benefiting both since 2 < 3.5 < 4.

options_template.text: Both NorCal's and SoCal's CPFs pivot further outward simultaneously because a higher TOT raises global output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (TOT-Expands-Production Fallacy): Total specialized output (40X, 120Y) is fixed; changing TOT redistributes gains between the two partners rather than expanding both CPFs simultaneously.

options_template.text: SoCal's CPF pivots further outward while NorCal's CPF pivots inward because SoCal now receives more Avocados per Microchip.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Exporter-Importer Swap): NorCal exports Microchips (X) and receives Avocados (Y); raising the price of X from 3Y to 3.5Y helps NorCal and makes X more expensive for SoCal.

options_template.text: SoCal's CPF collapses strictly inside its domestic PPF, forcing SoCal into autarky immediately.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Threshold-Breach Misreading): Because TOT = 3.5Y still lies strictly below SoCal's domestic cost of 4Y per 1X, SoCal still gains from trade and its CPF stays outside its PPF.

questions.topic: Linear PPF Attainability & Unrealized Output
questions.title: Classifying a Production Bundle and Measuring Unrealized Output
questions.prompt_template: An economy's linear PPF between Cloud Servers (X) and Medical Scanners (Y) is given by Y = 120 - 3X. Classify the production bundle (25 Cloud Servers, 30 Medical Scanners) and quantify any unrealized Medical Scanner output holding Cloud Servers fixed at 25.

hints.text: Substitute X = 25 into the PPF equation Y = 120 - 3X to find the maximum feasible Medical Scanners (Y_max).
Compare actual output Y = 30 against Y_max(25), and compute the difference Y_max(25) - 30.

options_template.text: Attainable but inefficient, with 45 Medical Scanners of unrealized output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Maximum-as-Gap Fallacy): Y_max(25) = 120 - 3(25) = 45 is the total maximum feasible output at X = 25, not the unrealized gap; you must subtract actual output (30) to get 15.

options_template.text: Attainable but inefficient, with 15 Medical Scanners of unrealized output.
options_template.feedback: Correct. At X = 25, Y_max = 120 - 3(25) = 45 Medical Scanners. Since actual output (30) is below 45, the bundle lies inside the PPF with 45 - 30 = 15 Medical Scanners of unrealized output.

options_template.text: Attainable but inefficient, with 5 Medical Scanners of unrealized output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Axis-Unit Confusion): 5 is the unrealized gap in Cloud Servers holding Medical Scanners at 30 (since X_max(30) = 30, and 30 - 25 = 5), not the unrealized Medical Scanner output.

options_template.text: Unattainable, because the bundle exceeds maximum feasible output by 15 Medical Scanners.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inequality-Direction Error): Because actual Y (30) is less than Y_max (45), the economy is producing below capacity (inside the PPF), not above capacity.

questions.topic: Linear PPF Resource Constraint & Reciprocal OC
questions.title: Computing Both Opportunity Costs from an Implicit Linear PPF
questions.prompt_template: An economy's resource constraint between Electric Vehicles (X, thousands) and Grid Battery Packs (Y, thousands) is given by 4X + 2Y = 160. What are the constant opportunity costs of producing 1 Electric Vehicle and 1 Grid Battery Pack?

hints.text: First solve the resource constraint 4X + 2Y = 160 explicitly for Y as a function of X.
The magnitude of the slope |Delta Y / Delta X| gives the opportunity cost of 1X, and its reciprocal gives the opportunity cost of 1Y.

options_template.text: 2 Battery Packs per Electric Vehicle, and 0.5 Electric Vehicles per Battery Pack.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Rewriting 4X + 2Y = 160 gives Y = 80 - 2X. Thus OC_1X = |Delta Y / Delta X| = 2 Battery Packs, and OC_1Y = 1 / 2 = 0.5 Electric Vehicles.

options_template.text: 4 Battery Packs per Electric Vehicle, and 2 Electric Vehicles per Battery Pack.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Raw-Coefficient Fallacy): The coefficients 4 and 2 are resource weights in the implicit equation; you must divide by 2 to obtain the slope Y = 80 - 2X.

options_template.text: 0.5 Battery Packs per Electric Vehicle, and 2 Electric Vehicles per Battery Pack.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted-Slope Fallacy): This reverses the two opportunity costs by computing |Delta X / Delta Y| = 0.5 for Electric Vehicles instead of |Delta Y / Delta X| = 2.

options_template.text: 80 Battery Packs per Electric Vehicle, and 40 Electric Vehicles per Battery Pack.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intercept-as-Opportunity-Cost Fallacy): 80 and 40 are the maximum production intercepts, not per-unit opportunity costs (their ratio 80 / 40 = 2 gives OC_1X).

questions.topic: Total Opportunity Cost Along a Linear PPF
questions.title: Total Sacrifice Along a Linear PPF Between Two Points
questions.prompt_template: An economy operating on the linear PPF Y = 90 - 2.5X decides to increase production of Good X from X = 12 units to X = 20 units. What is the total opportunity cost of this expansion in terms of Good Y sacrificed?

hints.text: Calculate the gain in Good X (Delta X = 20 - 12), or evaluate Y at both endpoints X = 12 and X = 20.
Multiply the per-unit opportunity cost (2.5 units of Y per X) by Delta X = 8.

options_template.text: 40 units of Good Y.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Endpoint-Level Fallacy): Y(20) = 90 - 2.5(20) = 40 is the remaining quantity of Good Y produced at the new point, not the quantity of Good Y sacrificed (60 - 40 = 20).

options_template.text: 2.5 units of Good Y.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Per-Unit-vs-Total Cost Fallacy): 2.5 is the opportunity cost of 1 additional unit of X; expanding by 8 units of X sacrifices 8 x 2.5 = 20 units of Y.

options_template.text: 3.2 units of Good Y.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverse-Division Fallacy): Dividing Delta X = 8 by the slope 2.5 yields 3.2; you must multiply Delta X by the slope to find |Delta Y|.

options_template.text: 20 units of Good Y.
options_template.feedback: Correct. At X = 12, Y = 90 - 2.5(12) = 60; at X = 20, Y = 90 - 2.5(20) = 40. Expanding X by 8 units sacrifices 60 - 40 = 20 units of Good Y (8 x 2.5 = 20).

questions.topic: Discrete Opportunity Cost on a Concave PPF
questions.title: Computing Per-Unit Opportunity Cost on a Quadratic PPF
questions.prompt_template: An economy's concave PPF between Autonomous Drones (X, thousands) and Grain (Y, thousand tons) is given by Y = 144 - X^2 for 0 <= X <= 12. If the economy moves along the frontier from X = 4 thousand drones to X = 8 thousand drones, what is the per-unit opportunity cost of 1 additional drone over this interval?

hints.text: Evaluate Y at both endpoints: Y(4) = 144 - 16 and Y(8) = 144 - 64.
Compute the discrete per-unit opportunity cost using |Y(8) - Y(4)| / (8 - 4).

options_template.text: 48 tons of grain per drone.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total-vs-Per-Unit Fallacy): 48 thousand tons is the total grain sacrificed across all 4 thousand new drones; dividing by Delta X = 4 gives 12 tons per drone.

options_template.text: 10 tons of grain per drone.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Endpoint-Ratio Fallacy): Dividing Y(8) / 8 = 80 / 8 = 10 computes the average ratio of output levels at the endpoint rather than the marginal change |Delta Y / Delta X|.

options_template.text: 12 tons of grain per drone.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Moving from (4, 128) to (8, 80) gains Delta X = 4 thousand drones while sacrificing |Delta Y| = 48 thousand tons of grain, so OC = 48 / 4 = 12 tons of grain per drone.

options_template.text: 16 tons of grain per drone.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Right-Endpoint Derivative Fallacy): 2(8) = 16 is the instantaneous MRT evaluated solely at the right endpoint X = 8, rather than the discrete per-unit OC over the interval [4, 8].

questions.topic: Comparing Rising Opportunity Costs Across Intervals
questions.title: Quantifying the Escalation in Per-Unit Opportunity Cost
questions.prompt_template: An economy's discrete concave production schedule contains bundles A(0, 200), B(5, 190), C(10, 165), D(15, 125), E(20, 70), and F(25, 0) for Good X and Good Y. By how many units of Good Y does the per-unit opportunity cost of Good X increase when comparing the move from D to E against the move from A to B?

hints.text: Compute the per-unit opportunity cost |Delta Y / Delta X| separately for A -> B and for D -> E.
Remember that Delta X = 5 in both intervals, then take the difference between the two per-unit costs.

options_template.text: 9.0 units of Good Y per unit of Good X.
options_template.feedback: Correct. From A to B, OC = |190 - 200| / 5 = 2.0Y per X. From D to E, OC = |70 - 125| / 5 = 11.0Y per X. Thus the per-unit opportunity cost rises by 11.0 - 2.0 = 9.0 units of Y per X.

options_template.text: 45.0 units of Good Y per unit of Good X.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unscaled-Difference Fallacy): 55 - 10 = 45 compares total Y sacrificed per 5-unit step without dividing by Delta X = 5 to express the result per unit of X.

options_template.text: 11.0 units of Good Y per unit of Good X.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Level-vs-Change Fallacy): 11.0 is the per-unit opportunity cost during the D -> E step itself, not the increase above the A -> B baseline of 2.0.

options_template.text: 3.5 units of Good Y per unit of Good X.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Output-Ratio Fallacy): 70 / 20 = 3.5 takes the ratio of total output levels at bundle E rather than comparing marginal opportunity costs across intervals.

questions.topic: Calculus Extension: MRT and Marginal Cost Ratio
questions.title: Using MRT_XY = -dY/dX = MC_X / MC_Y to Solve for MC_X
questions.prompt_template: An economy faces the smooth concave PPF Y = 100 - X^2 on 0 <= X <= 10. At the efficient production point where X = 4, suppose the marginal production cost of Good Y is MC_Y = $16. Using MRT_XY = -dY/dX = MC_X / MC_Y, what are MRT_XY(4) and the marginal cost MC_X?

hints.text: Differentiate Y = 100 - X^2 with respect to X and take the negative to find MRT_XY(X) = 2X.
Evaluate MRT_XY at X = 4, then solve MRT_XY = MC_X / MC_Y for MC_X.

options_template.text: MRT_XY(4) = 4 and MC_X = $64.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Missing Power-Rule Factor): The derivative of -X^2 is -2X (not -X), so MRT_XY(4) = 2(4) = 8 rather than 4.

options_template.text: MRT_XY(4) = 8 and MC_X = $2.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Marginal-Cost Ratio): Setting MRT = MC_Y / MC_X yields 16 / 8 = $2; the correct identity is MRT_XY = MC_X / MC_Y, so MC_X = 8 x $16 = $128.

options_template.text: MRT_XY(4) = 16 and MC_X = $256.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Undifferentiated-Term Fallacy): Plugging X = 4 into X^2 gives 16 instead of taking the first derivative 2X = 8.

options_template.text: MRT_XY(4) = 8 and MC_X = $128.
options_template.feedback: Correct. MRT_XY(X) = -d(100 - X^2)/dX = 2X, so MRT_XY(4) = 8. Since MRT_XY = MC_X / MC_Y, MC_X = 8 x $16 = $128.

questions.topic: Identifying Absolute vs. Comparative Advantage
questions.title: Separating Absolute and Comparative Advantage from Linear Capacities
questions.prompt_template: Using identical annual resources along linear PPFs, Region East can produce at most 80 million Microchips (X) or 200 million Avocados (Y), while Region West can produce at most 50 million Microchips (X) or 100 million Avocados (Y). Which statement accurately identifies each region's domestic opportunity costs and comparative advantage?

hints.text: Compute OC_1X = Max Y / Max X and OC_1Y = Max X / Max Y for both East and West.
Assign comparative advantage in each good to the region with the lower domestic opportunity cost—even if the other region has higher maximum output.

options_template.text: East has comparative advantage in both goods because it can produce more Microchips (80 > 50) and more Avocados (200 > 100).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Absolute-Equals-Comparative Fallacy): Higher maximum output gives East an absolute advantage in both goods, but comparative advantage is determined solely by lower relative opportunity cost.

options_template.text: West has comparative advantage in Microchips (OC_1X = 2.0Y < East's 2.5Y), while East has comparative advantage in Avocados (OC_1Y = 0.4X < West's 0.5X).
options_template.feedback: Correct. East's OC_1X = 200/80 = 2.5Y (OC_1Y = 0.4X) while West's OC_1X = 100/50 = 2.0Y (OC_1Y = 0.5X). Thus West specializes in Microchips and East specializes in Avocados.

options_template.text: East has comparative advantage in Microchips (OC_1X = 0.4Y) and West has comparative advantage in Avocados (OC_1Y = 2.0X).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted-Ratio Fallacy): This divides Max X by Max Y to label OC_1X, reversing the units; sacrificing 200Y for 80X costs 2.5Y per Microchip, not 0.4Y.

options_template.text: East has comparative advantage in Microchips (OC_1X = 2.5Y > 2.0Y) and West has comparative advantage in Avocados (OC_1Y = 0.5X > 0.4X).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Higher-Cost-Selection Fallacy): Comparative advantage belongs to the producer with the LOWER opportunity cost, not the higher opportunity cost.

questions.topic: Mutually Beneficial Terms of Trade Bounds
questions.title: Establishing Valid Terms of Trade Bounds for Good Y
questions.prompt_template: Country A faces the linear PPF Y = 100 - 2X, and Country B faces the linear PPF Y = 200 - 5X. If both countries specialize according to comparative advantage, what is the range of mutually beneficial Terms of Trade (TOT) for 1 unit of Good Y (expressed in units of Good X)?

hints.text: First read OC_1X from each linear PPF slope, then take the reciprocal to obtain each country's domestic opportunity cost of 1 unit of Good Y.
Valid TOT for 1 unit of Good Y must lie strictly between the exporter's OC_1Y and the importer's OC_1Y.

options_template.text: 2.0 units of X < TOT_1Y < 5.0 units of X.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Uninverted-Good-X Bounds): 2 and 5 are the domestic opportunity costs of 1 unit of Good X (in terms of Y); for 1 unit of Good Y you must take the reciprocals 1/5 = 0.2X and 1/2 = 0.5X.

options_template.text: 0.5 units of X < TOT_1Y < 2.0 units of X.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Country Cross-Good Mixing): 0.5X is Country A's OC_1Y while 2.0Y is Country A's OC_1X; TOT bounds must compare the same good across the two different countries.

options_template.text: 0.2 units of X < TOT_1Y < 0.5 units of X.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Country A's OC_1Y = 1/2 = 0.5X and Country B's OC_1Y = 1/5 = 0.2X. Country B exports Good Y at any price strictly above 0.2X, and Country A imports Good Y at any price strictly below 0.5X.

options_template.text: 0.2 units of X < TOT_1Y < 5.0 units of X.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Partner Reciprocal Mixing): 0.2X and 5.0Y are Country B's own reciprocal opportunity costs; the upper bound must be Country A's domestic cost of Y (0.5X).

questions.topic: Joint Production Gains from Complete Specialization
questions.title: Calculating Combined Output Gains Under Complete Specialization
questions.prompt_template: Region Delta has linear PPF Y = 90 - 3X (autarky bundle A_D = (15X, 45Y)), and Region Sierra has linear PPF Y = 80 - 2X (autarky bundle A_S = (20X, 40Y)). If each region specializes completely in its comparative-advantage good, what is the combined net production gain relative to autarky?

hints.text: Determine each region's OC_1X from the slope, then sum their autarky outputs (15 + 20, 45 + 40).
Have the lower-OC_1X region produce only X (its horizontal intercept) and the other region produce only Y (its vertical intercept), then subtract total autarky output.

options_template.text: +5 units of Good X and +5 units of Good Y.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Combined autarky output is (35X, 85Y). Sierra has lower OC_1X (2Y < 3Y) and specializes at (40X, 0Y); Delta specializes in Y at (0X, 90Y). Combined output rises to (40X, 90Y), a net gain of +5X and +5Y.

options_template.text: +40 units of Good X and +90 units of Good Y.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total-Output-as-Gain Fallacy): (40X, 90Y) is total combined specialized production; you must subtract the combined autarky output of (35X, 85Y) to isolate the net gain.

options_template.text: -5 units of Good X and -5 units of Good Y.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reverse-Specialization Fallacy): Having Delta specialize in X (30X) and Sierra in Y (80Y) reverses comparative advantage, shrinking combined output below autarky by 5 units of each good.

options_template.text: +20 units of Good X and +45 units of Good Y.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Region-Only Gain Fallacy): Adding Sierra's +20X gain and Delta's +45Y gain ignores that Sierra ceases producing 40Y and Delta ceases producing 15X when specializing.

questions.topic: Post-Trade Consumption and Gains Over Autarky
questions.title: Verifying Post-Trade Consumption Bundle and Net Welfare Gains
questions.prompt_template: Region Valley (PPF: Y = 120 - 2X; autarky A_V = (30X, 60Y)) and Region Coast (PPF: Y = 200 - 4X; autarky A_C = (25X, 100Y)) specialize completely according to comparative advantage. Valley then exports 28 units of X to Coast at TOT = 3Y per 1X. What is Coast's post-trade consumption bundle, and what is Coast's net gain over autarky?

hints.text: Identify which region specializes in Y (200Y) and compute the total units of Y Coast sends to Valley for 28X at TOT = 3Y/1X.
Subtract exported Y from Coast's specialized output (200Y), then compare Coast's post-trade bundle to A_C(25X, 100Y).

options_template.text: (32X, 84Y), gaining +2X and +24Y over autarky.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Trading-Partner Swap): (32X, 84Y) and (+2X, +24Y) are Region Valley's post-trade bundle and net gains, not Region Coast's.

options_template.text: (28X, 116Y), gaining +3X and +16Y over autarky.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Coast specializes in Y at (0X, 200Y), imports 28X, and exports 28 x 3 = 84Y, keeping 200 - 84 = 116Y. Relative to autarky (25X, 100Y), Coast gains +3X and +16Y.

options_template.text: (28X, 172Y), gaining +3X and +72Y over autarky.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (1-for-1 Barter Fallacy): Subtracting 28 instead of 28 x 3 = 84 from Coast's 200Y ignores the agreed Terms of Trade of 3Y per 1X.

options_template.text: (28X, 16Y), gaining +3X and losing 84Y relative to autarky.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Autarky-Baseline-Export Error): Subtracting 84Y exported from Coast's autarky output of 100Y forgets that Coast specialized completely to produce 200Y before trading.

questions.topic: CPF Intercept and Distance Beyond Domestic PPF
questions.title: Measuring the Vertical CPF Intercept and Excess Above Autarky PPF
questions.prompt_template: Region Bay has linear PPF Y = 100 - 2X (maximum 50X or 100Y). Bay specializes completely in Good X at (50, 0) and trades at TOT = 3.5Y per 1X. What is the vertical intercept of Bay's Consumption Possibilities Frontier (CPF), and if Bay exports 20X, by how many units of Good Y does its post-trade bundle exceed its domestic PPF at X = 30?

hints.text: Multiply Bay's maximum X production (50) by TOT = 3.5 to find the vertical CPF intercept.
At X = 30 (after exporting 20X), compare imported Y (20 x 3.5) against domestic Y_PPF(30) = 100 - 2(30).

options_template.text: Vertical CPF intercept = 175Y; exceeds domestic PPF by 70Y.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total-Import-as-Excess Fallacy): 70Y is Bay's total imported Y (20 x 3.5); you must subtract domestic Y_PPF(30) = 40Y to find the 30Y excess beyond the PPF.

options_template.text: Vertical CPF intercept = 175Y; exceeds domestic PPF by 75Y.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intercept-Gap Substitution): 175 - 100 = 75Y is the vertical gap between the CPF and PPF at X = 0, not at Bay's post-trade consumption point X = 30.

options_template.text: Vertical CPF intercept = 175Y; exceeds domestic PPF by 30Y.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Exporting all 50X at TOT = 3.5 yields a CPF intercept of 50 x 3.5 = 175Y. Exporting 20X yields (30X, 70Y), whereas domestic Y_PPF(30) = 100 - 2(30) = 40Y, an excess of 70 - 40 = 30Y.

options_template.text: Vertical CPF intercept = 350Y; exceeds domestic PPF by 30Y.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong-Intercept Multiplication): Multiplying Y_max = 100 by TOT = 3.5 gives 350Y; Bay specializes in X (50 units), so maximum obtainable Y is 50 x 3.5 = 175Y.

questions.topic: Sector-Biased Innovation Quantitative Recalculation
questions.title: Recalculating Opportunity Cost and Feasible Output After Biased Growth
questions.prompt_template: An economy's initial linear PPF between Software (X) and Grain (Y) is Y = 120 - 4X (maximum 30X or 120Y). A sector-specific innovation doubles maximum Software output to 60X while leaving maximum Grain output unchanged at 120Y. What are the new per-unit opportunity cost of 1 unit of Software and the new maximum feasible Grain output when producing X = 25 units of Software?

hints.text: Write the new linear PPF passing through intercepts (0, 120) and (60, 0) to find the new slope.
Substitute X = 25 into the new PPF equation to find Y_max(25).

options_template.text: New OC_1X = 8 Grain; X = 25 is unattainable with positive Grain.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direct-Proportionality OC Fallacy): Doubling productivity in Software HALVES the opportunity cost of Software from 4Y to 2Y rather than doubling it to 8Y.

options_template.text: New OC_1X = 2 Grain; maximum Grain at X = 25 remains 20 units.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Spillover Fallacy): Even though Grain technology did not change, producing 25 Software now takes half as many resources, freeing inputs to raise maximum Grain from 20 to 70 units.

options_template.text: New OC_1X = 4 Grain; maximum Grain at X = 25 rises to 140 units.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Balanced-Shift Confusion): Doubling both intercepts to Y = 240 - 4X contradicts the prompt's condition that maximum Grain output remains unchanged at 120Y.

options_template.text: New OC_1X = 2 Grain; maximum Grain at X = 25 rises to 70 units.
options_template.feedback: Correct. With intercepts (0, 120) and (60, 0), the new PPF is Y = 120 - 2X, halving OC_1X to 2 Grain. At X = 25, Y_max(25) = 120 - 2(25) = 70 Grain (up from 20 Grain previously).

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Bring It Home: California Specialization vs. Autarky
questions.title: Why California Imports Coffee and Laptops Despite World-Class Resources
questions.prompt_template: California possesses highly productive farmland, top engineering talent, and abundant venture capital—meaning it could technically grow coffee beans in climate-controlled greenhouses and assemble every laptop sold in the state. Using the PPF and comparative advantage framework, why would enforcing self-sufficiency in coffee and laptop assembly make Californians poorer?

hints.text: Ask what high-value outputs California would have to sacrifice to pull land, water, and engineers into coffee greenhouses and hardware assembly.
Connect that high domestic opportunity cost to the difference between California's domestic PPF and its post-trade CPF.

options_template.text: Because California lacks an absolute advantage in any agricultural or technology sector and cannot physically produce coffee or electronics.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Absolute-Disadvantage Assumption): The chapter explicitly notes California could technically produce both goods; the reason it imports them is comparative disadvantage (high opportunity cost), not physical impossibility.

options_template.text: Because diverting scarce land, water, and engineering talent away from almonds, wine, software, and chip design imposes a steep domestic opportunity cost, collapsing California's CPF back onto its domestic PPF.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Specializing where California's relative opportunity cost is lowest and trading for coffee and consumer electronics expands California's CPF strictly beyond what domestic self-sufficiency can deliver.

options_template.text: Because importing goods automatically shifts California's domestic PPF outward every year without requiring capital investment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Trade-Shifts-PPF Confusion): Trade pivots the Consumption Possibilities Frontier (CPF) outside a given domestic PPF; it does not directly shift the domestic production boundary itself.

options_template.text: Because greenhouse coffee farming exhibits constant opportunity cost, violating the Law of Increasing Opportunity Cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Curvature-Violation Misdiagnosis): Gains from trade hold under both constant and increasing opportunity costs; the welfare loss from autarky comes from ignoring lower-cost trading partners.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Central Valley Land, Water, and Grid Trade-Offs
questions.title: Evaluating Policy Scenarios in California's Central Valley PPF
questions.prompt_template: Consider California's Central Valley PPF between utility-scale solar power generation and irrigated specialty agriculture (almonds, tomatoes, pistachios), which compete for flat acreage, senior water allocations, and grid transmission capacity. Which policy pairing correctly maps onto (1) eliminating an interior inefficiency, (2) moving along the PPF, and (3) shifting the PPF outward?

hints.text: Match each action to whether it uses idle land/grid capacity, converts active land from one use to another, or creates brand-new water/grid infrastructure.
Remember Figure 2.1's interior point U, frontier point A, and unattainable point W.

options_template.text: (1) Building new desalination plants; (2) idling farmland during a drought; (3) converting retired farmland into solar-plus-storage.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Scrambled PPF Mechanics): Desalination expands total water capacity (outward shift), idling farmland creates an interior inefficiency rather than a frontier move, and converting land moves along the frontier.

options_template.text: (1) Converting irrigated orchards into solar farms; (2) building high-voltage transmission lines; (3) leaving drought-idled fields unused.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift-and-Movement Misclassification): Converting active land moves along the PPF, building new transmission shifts the PPF outward, and leaving fields idle leaves the economy inside the PPF.

options_template.text: (1) Resolving transmission bottlenecks to reactivate idled capacity; (2) converting retired agricultural acreage into solar-plus-storage; (3) constructing new desalination and high-voltage transmission infrastructure.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Reactivating idle capacity moves from interior point U toward the frontier; converting agricultural acreage to solar moves along the frontier; adding desalination and grid infrastructure shifts the PPF outward toward previously unattainable bundles like W.

options_template.text: (1) Mandating simultaneous expansion of both crops and solar with fixed water; (2) reducing labor hours; (3) raising electricity prices.
