options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unattainable-Mandate Fallacy): Simultaneously expanding both outputs beyond fixed water and grid limits is physically unattainable without new infrastructure.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Allocative vs. Productive Efficiency Policy Critique
questions.title: Critiquing a Full-Employment Industrial Quota Policy
questions.prompt_template: A regional planner boasts that a new industrial mandate achieved 100% factory and labor utilization on the economy's PPF, yet citizens complain of acute shortages of housing and medical care alongside massive warehouses overflowing with unwanted consumer gadgets. What economic critique best diagnoses this policy failure?

hints.text: Ask whether operating on the PPF is sufficient for economic efficiency.
Use the Clear It Up distinction between productive efficiency and allocative efficiency (MB = MC).

options_template.text: The mandate achieved productive efficiency by eliminating idle resources, but severely violated allocative efficiency by choosing a frontier bundle where MB != MC relative to society's actual preferences.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Reaching the PPF ensures zero resource waste (productive efficiency), but social welfare also requires selecting the single frontier point where marginal benefit equals marginal cost (allocative efficiency).

options_template.text: The mandate failed productive efficiency because producing unpopular goods necessarily pushes the economy inside its PPF.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Preference-Location Conflation): Productive efficiency depends strictly on full, non-wasteful resource utilization on the frontier, regardless of how much consumers value the mix.

options_template.text: The mandate pushed the economy outside its PPF into an unattainable zone, causing shortages of housing and medical care.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shortage-as-Exterior-Point Confusion): Shortages of specific goods alongside surpluses of unwanted goods reflect a mischosen point along the PPF, not production beyond physical capacity.

options_template.text: The mandate proved that scarcity no longer binds once an economy reaches 100% employment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Full-Employment-Eliminates-Scarcity Fallacy): Scarcity binds most sharply at full employment on the PPF, where producing unwanted gadgets directly costs forgone housing and healthcare.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: AI Data Center Buildout: Short-Run vs. Long-Run
questions.title: Analyzing AI Infrastructure Expansion Across Time Horizons
questions.prompt_template: As firms rapidly expand AI data centers, they initially tap flexible semiconductor wafer capacity and electrical engineers from smartphones and automotive chips, but further rapid buildout forces cannibalization of specialized industrial lines before new fabrication plants, trained engineers, and next-generation lithography come online years later. Which PPF synthesis best explains both phases?

hints.text: Separate the immediate short-run reallocation (fixed fabs and engineers) from the multi-year capital and technology expansion.
Connect short-run specialized bottlenecks to concave curvature, and multi-year investment to outward shifts.

options_template.text: Both phases represent constant opportunity cost along a fixed linear PPF because semiconductor wafers are perfectly interchangeable across every industry.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Perfect-Adaptability Fallacy): Specialized cleanrooms, high-bandwidth memory fabs, and electrical transformers exhibit imperfect adaptability in the short run, and new fabs shift the PPF in the long run.

options_template.text: The short-run phase shifts the PPF inward due to cannibalization, while the long-run phase merely moves the economy back onto the original PPF.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reallocation-as-Contraction Error): Cannibalizing industrial lines is a high-opportunity-cost movement along a concave PPF, not an inward capacity shift, and new fabs expand capacity beyond PPF_0.

options_template.text: The short-run phase represents operating inside the PPF with idle engineers, while the long-run phase moves along a fixed frontier.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Short-Run/Long-Run Dynamics): Pulling scarce engineers from active auto and smartphone lines occurs along a capacity-constrained frontier, while multi-year fab construction shifts the frontier outward.

options_template.text: In the short run, imperfect factor adaptability generates rising marginal opportunity costs along a concave PPF; in the long run, new fabs, human capital training, and next-gen lithography shift the PPF outward.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Fixed short-run infrastructure forces increasingly costly reallocations along the concave frontier, whereas multi-year physical capital, human capital, and technological investments shift PPF_0 outward to PPF_1.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Recovery Policy vs. Supply-Side Growth Policy
questions.title: Evaluating Short-Run Stabilization vs. Long-Run Capacity Investments
questions.prompt_template: During a recession with high unemployment and idle manufacturing plants, Policy Advisor X advocates temporary spending to rehire laid-off workers into existing factories, while Policy Advisor Y advocates multi-year investments in STEM vocational training, power grids, and chip research. How does the PPF model classify the distinct effect of each policy?

hints.text: Identify where the economy starts during a recession (inside the PPF).
Distinguish putting existing idle resources back to work from expanding total maximum potential output.

options_template.text: Advisor X's policy shifts the PPF outward immediately, whereas Advisor Y's policy moves the economy from inside the PPF to the frontier.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Swapped Policy Horizons): Rehiring idle workers moves an interior point toward the existing PPF (recovery), whereas training, grids, and R&D expand future capacity (outward shift).

options_template.text: Advisor X's policy promotes short-run recovery by moving the economy from an interior point toward the existing PPF, whereas Advisor Y's policy promotes long-run economic growth by shifting the entire PPF outward.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Reducing cyclical unemployment restores utilization of existing capacity; human capital, physical infrastructure, and technological innovation expand the frontier itself.

options_template.text: Both policies merely move the economy along an unchanged PPF without changing total output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Output Fallacy): Moving from an interior point to the frontier increases output of both goods, and shifting the PPF outward expands maximum output even further.

options_template.text: Advisor X's policy is ineffective because an economy inside its PPF faces infinite opportunity costs when expanding output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Interior-Cost Inversion): Inside the PPF, idle resources allow output expansion with zero opportunity cost in the other sector, making recovery policies capable of raising total output.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Intertemporal Investment Policy Trade-Off
questions.title: Weighing Current Living Standards Against Future Growth Capacity
questions.prompt_template: Policymakers in a developing economy debate diverting a larger share of current GDP away from immediate consumer goods toward public health clinics, vocational schools, and automated factories. What real economic trade-off does the PPF framework reveal about this choice?

hints.text: Identify both the immediate opportunity cost today and the dynamic shift over future decades.
Remember that public health, education, and factories build human and physical capital.

options_template.text: There is zero opportunity cost today because investments in human and physical capital instantly expand current consumer output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Free-Lunch Investment Fallacy): Along today's PPF, allocating more resources to capital and education requires sacrificing immediate consumer goods today.

options_template.text: The policy permanently reduces living standards because factories and clinics cannot produce consumer goods in the future.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Static-Horizon Trap): Expanding physical and human capital shifts future PPFs outward, enabling higher consumption of consumer goods in future periods than would otherwise be possible.

options_template.text: Society incurs an immediate opportunity cost in forgone current consumption along today's PPF in exchange for a faster outward shift of future PPFs via physical and human capital accumulation.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Moving along today's PPF toward capital goods and human capital sacrifices current consumption today in order to expand the economy's future productive capacity for all goods.

options_template.text: The policy moves the economy strictly inside its current PPF because consumer spending falls.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Lower-Consumption-as-Inefficiency Fallacy): Shifting resources from consumer goods into productive capital keeps the economy fully employed on its frontier.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Sector-Biased Innovation Spillover Effect
questions.title: How Single-Sector Innovation Can Increase Output of Both Goods
questions.prompt_template: A skeptical official argues that an agricultural biotechnology breakthrough improving only wheat yields (Good X) cannot possibly help a nation produce more hospital care (Good Y) because medical technology did not change. Using Figure 2.3 Panel (b), how should an economist refute this claim?

hints.text: Look at a horizontal line at the economy's original wheat output level before and after the horizontal intercept pivots outward.
Ask how many workers and resources are now needed to grow the exact same amount of wheat as before.

options_template.text: Higher wheat productivity allows the nation to grow its original wheat harvest using fewer workers and resources, freeing those saved inputs to expand hospital care—allowing more of both goods simultaneously.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Pivoting the wheat intercept outward places every prior interior-mix point strictly inside the new PPF, enabling society to expand both wheat and hospital care at the same time.

options_template.text: Biotechnology in wheat automatically shifts the vertical hospital-care intercept upward even when zero wheat is produced.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Vertical-Intercept Misreading): When X = 0 (zero wheat produced), wheat technology is unused, so the vertical hospital-care intercept stays fixed; gains in Y occur at all positive levels of X.

options_template.text: The official is completely correct: unless medical technology also improves, hospital output can never increase above its pre-innovation level.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Spillover Fallacy): Resource reallocation creates real cross-sector spillovers whenever productivity rises in any industry where the economy actively produces.

options_template.text: Hospital care increases only because the biotechnology breakthrough forces the economy into autarky.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Irrelevant Autarky Attribution): The cross-sector gain arises purely from domestic resource reallocation along a pivoted PPF, independent of trade isolation.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Global Semiconductor Supply Chain Policy
questions.title: Opportunity Cost of Mandating End-to-End Semiconductor Autarky
questions.prompt_template: In the global semiconductor industry, Silicon Valley clusters hold a comparative advantage in processor architecture and electronic design automation (EDA) software, while East Asian hubs hold a comparative advantage in wafer fabrication and advanced chip packaging. If each region banned cross-border trade and forced an isolated end-to-end domestic supply chain, what would the Ricardian model predict?

hints.text: Compare specialized cross-border production plus trade against isolated autarky in both regions.
Think about how each region's Consumption Possibilities Frontier changes when specialization is prohibited.

options_template.text: Global computing power would expand because duplicating cleanrooms and design hubs doubles total efficiency.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Duplication-as-Efficiency Fallacy): Forcing each region to produce high-opportunity-cost stages sacrifices comparative advantage and shrinks combined global computing output.

options_template.text: Only the region with lower absolute productivity would suffer, while the higher-productivity region would expand its CPF.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (One-Sided Trade Fallacy): Under comparative advantage, trade expands BOTH partners' CPFs; reverting to autarky contracts consumption possibilities for both regions.

options_template.text: Each region's domestic PPF would collapse to the origin, making semiconductor production physically impossible.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total-Collapse Hyperbole): Autarky does not eliminate domestic production capacity; it merely traps each region on its own domestic PPF instead of the higher CPF.

options_template.text: Each region would divert specialized talent and capital into higher-opportunity-cost stages, reducing combined global processor output and collapsing both regions' CPFs back to their domestic PPFs.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Breaking comparative-advantage specialization forces inefficient domestic substitution, shrinking total global output and eliminating the CPF expansion generated by trade.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Refuting the Absolute Advantage Protectionist Argument
questions.title: Why High-Productivity Economies Still Gain from Trading with Lower-Productivity Partners
questions.prompt_template: A commentator argues: 'Because our nation's workers produce more output per hour than our neighbor's workers in EVERY single industry, trading with them can only drag down our standard of living.' What is the fundamental flaw in this argument?

hints.text: Recall the Clear It Up rule distinguishing absolute advantage from comparative advantage.
Check Country Alpha and Country Beta in the chapter's Check Your Understanding problem, where Alpha held absolute advantage in both goods.

options_template.text: It is mathematically impossible for one nation to have higher output per worker in every industry.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Absolute-Advantage Impossibility Myth): A capital-rich, technologically advanced nation can easily hold an absolute advantage in every sector; what is impossible is holding a comparative advantage in both.

options_template.text: High-productivity nations gain from trade only if they force Terms of Trade strictly below their own domestic opportunity cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Below-Cost Export Fallacy): Exporting below domestic opportunity cost would cause losses; an exporter gains whenever TOT lies strictly ABOVE its own domestic OC.

options_template.text: It confuses absolute advantage with comparative advantage; as long as relative opportunity costs differ, the high-productivity nation gains by specializing where its productivity edge is largest and importing where its edge is smallest.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Even with absolute advantage in every industry, specializing in the lowest-opportunity-cost sector and trading at mutually beneficial TOT expands the high-productivity nation's CPF.

options_template.text: Trade benefits a high-productivity nation only when its domestic opportunity costs are identical to its neighbor's.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Identical-OC Fallacy): Identical domestic opportunity costs eliminate comparative advantage and leave zero potential gains from Ricardian trade.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Tariffs, Transport Costs, and the Ricardian TOT Window
questions.title: How Trade Frictions Erode the Mutually Beneficial TOT Range
questions.prompt_template: The baseline Ricardian model assumes zero transportation costs and zero tariffs. Suppose NorCal's domestic OC of 1 Microchip is 2 Avocados, SoCal's domestic OC is 4 Avocados, and a new regional tariff plus shipping friction adds a resource wedge equivalent to 2.5 Avocados per Microchip traded. What is the predicted economic outcome?

hints.text: Compare the size of the total opportunity-cost gap between the two regions (4 - 2 = 2 Avocados) against the trade wedge (2.5 Avocados).
Can any price allow NorCal to net more than 2 Avocados while SoCal pays less than 4 Avocados?

options_template.text: Trade volume doubles because both regions must export more units to cover the tariff and shipping wedge.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Boosts-Volume Fallacy): Trade frictions raise the effective cost of exchanging goods; when the wedge exceeds the entire OC spread, voluntary trade ceases.

options_template.text: Mutually beneficial trade collapses completely and both regions revert to autarky, because the 2.5-Avocado wedge exceeds the entire 2-Avocado spread between their domestic opportunity costs.
options_template.feedback: Correct. For NorCal to net > 2Y after a 2.5Y wedge, SoCal would have to pay > 4.5Y per Microchip—exceeding SoCal's domestic cost of 4Y. Thus the friction destroys the mutually beneficial TOT window.

options_template.text: SoCal switches to exporting Microchips to NorCal so that neither region pays the transport wedge.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Comparative-Advantage Reversal): Shipping costs and tariffs do not invert underlying domestic opportunity costs; SoCal still faces a 4Y cost per Microchip.

options_template.text: Trade continues at TOT = 3Y per Microchip with zero loss in consumption possibilities for either region.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Frictionless-Trade Illusion): A real resource wedge of 2.5Y cannot be ignored; at any delivered price SoCal will pay (< 4Y), NorCal receives less than 1.5Y (< its domestic OC of 2Y).

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Distributional Effects of Terms of Trade Bargaining
questions.title: How Shifting Terms of Trade Redistributes Surplus Between Partners
questions.prompt_template: In the NorCal (OC_1X = 2Y) and SoCal (OC_1X = 4Y) model, mutually beneficial trade occurs whenever 2Y < TOT < 4Y. Suppose world demand shifts so the equilibrium TOT settles at 3.9Y per 1X instead of 3.0Y per 1X. How should a policy analyst evaluate the welfare impact on SoCal compared to autarky and compared to TOT = 3.0Y?

hints.text: Evaluate SoCal's welfare against TWO benchmarks: first against autarky (4Y per 1X), and second against the earlier TOT of 3.0Y per 1X.
Remember that any TOT strictly below 4Y still saves SoCal Avocados relative to self-sufficiency.

options_template.text: SoCal captures a much smaller share of the gains from trade than at TOT = 3.0Y (while NorCal captures more), yet SoCal is still strictly better off than in autarky because 3.9Y < 4.0Y.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Moving TOT closer to SoCal's domestic cost (4Y) transfers most of the trade surplus to NorCal, but because 3.9Y remains below 4Y, SoCal still obtains Microchips cheaper than in autarky.

options_template.text: SoCal is now strictly worse off than in autarky and should immediately ban all Microchip imports from NorCal.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Relative-Share-as-Absolute-Loss Fallacy): Receiving a smaller share of joint gains is not the same as suffering a net loss relative to autarky; at 3.9Y < 4Y, trade still expands SoCal's CPF.

options_template.text: Both NorCal and SoCal lose equally because any deviation from the midpoint TOT = 3.0Y destroys total specialization gains.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Midpoint-Optimality Myth): Complete specialization still yields the exact same total combined output at any TOT in (2, 4); moving away from 3.0 simply redistributes surplus between partners.

options_template.text: SoCal captures nearly 100% of the gains from trade because TOT = 3.9Y is closest to SoCal's domestic opportunity cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surplus-Proximity Inversion): A trading partner gains MORE when TOT is FARTHER from its own domestic opportunity cost and closer to its partner's cost.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Synthesizing Concave PPFs with Comparative Advantage
questions.title: Why Increasing Opportunity Cost Leads to Incomplete Specialization in Practice
questions.prompt_template: In the simple linear-PPF Ricardian model, trading regions specialize 100% in a single good. Yet in real-world economies—such as California producing software and microchips while still maintaining substantial domestic agriculture—nations typically engage in incomplete specialization. Which synthesis of Sections 2.2 and 2.3 best explains this empirical pattern?

hints.text: Combine the concave PPF (rising marginal opportunity cost) with the rule that a region expands exports only while its domestic OC is below the world TOT.
Ask what happens to a region's domestic MRT_XY as it expands production of its export good along a bowed-out PPF.

options_template.text: Real-world nations do not follow comparative advantage and instead choose output bundles strictly inside their PPFs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Irrationality Attribution): Incomplete specialization is a completely rational, efficient equilibrium along a concave PPF, not a sign of interior inefficiency.

options_template.text: Concave PPFs eliminate all gains from international trade, forcing countries to produce every good domestically.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Concavity-Eliminates-Trade Fallacy): Countries with bowed-out PPFs still capture substantial gains from trade and expand their CPFs; they simply stop specializing before hitting the axis intercept.

options_template.text: As a country expands its export industry along a concave PPF, its domestic opportunity cost falls to zero, causing exports to cease.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Decreasing-OC Inversion): Along a concave PPF, expanding an industry causes its domestic marginal opportunity cost to RISE, not fall.

options_template.text: Because real-world PPFs are concave due to imperfect factor adaptability, expanding the export sector drives its domestic marginal opportunity cost upward until it equals the world TOT, halting specialization before 100%.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Along a bowed-out PPF, MRT_XY rises as X expands; specialization stops profitably once domestic MRT_XY = TOT, leaving the region producing both goods while still gaining from trade.
